comfort. We integrate these perspectives with insights from psychology and neuro-architecture to discuss the
influence of space in the perceptions of thermal comfort beyond heat-exchange. We navigate the different studies
reviewed from a variety of fields within the social science and humanities and argue that cooling needs and
preferences are grounded in both cultural and corporeal perceptions, and are the result of individual subjective
experience of external stimuli within the body, culture, space, and society. We argue that placing humans at the

identify key areas of future research.

While the physiological angle can shed some light on the biophysical
mechanisms which determine thermal comfort, it is important to
establish caution towards a purely biological approach to thermal
comfort. For example, rather than focusing on gender differences in the
strictly biological sense, understanding the social constructions of
gender roles and everyday responsibilities can provide insight on how
habitus can influence thermal comfort rather than biological differences
per se. For example, social conventions which assign women the large
bulk of reproductive domestic tasks are still pervasive [51,52]; while
most women who have access to paid employment are typically per-
forming ‘caring’ jobs. In the UK, “The most common sectors of employment
for women are health and social work” particularly as nurses or teachers;
and the women working in mining, electricity and the construction
sector are few [53]. Clearly, the case is different in geographies with a
larger dependency on natural resource extraction that have a larger
participation of women in manual labour [54]. These examples help
spark some reflections on the gendered differentiation between outdoor
and indoor occupations, which can have an impact on the way women
